I have seen a kingfisher dart over it, and once a heron stood still in the reeds.

The stream that runs through the meadow. It is cold and fast, and the water is dark. I can see it from my tree, and I hear the water all night long. Sometimes I fly low over it, and the water reflects the moonlight. I do not drink from it, but I have seen voles drink from it. The stream is near, but I keep my distance. It is not safe.
A stream. It runs past the meadow and into the wood. I drink from it in the summer, but in the winter I go to the well under the ash.

The stream runs behind the oak. It is wide in places and narrow in others. The water is cold and the fish are silver. I do not drink from it, but I have seen voles drink from it. The water is loud at night.
A stream, running cold and fast under the meadow. I fly over it at dusk, and sometimes land on the bank. I drink from it.
The stream runs past the wood. It glistens in the dark. I drink from it.

A stream. It runs past the wood and through the meadow. I can hear it at night, the water sliding over stones and the rush of fish. I have seen it from the oak, and I have watched the water go down when the rain is heavy. The stream is near the wood, and it is where the voles come to drink. I have caught one there.

A stream, small and fast, runs through the meadow beyond the hollow. It is cold and clear, and the water reflects the moonlight. I have watched it from my perch, and sometimes I hear the water as it flows over stones. The stream is far from the meadow, but I can see its edge from my tree. I do not drink from it, but I have seen voles and shrews near its banks.

A stream. It runs by the east side of the meadow, and I drink from it on warm nights. The water is cold and clear, and the frogs jump in it when it rains. I have seen fish in it too, but I don't eat them. I wait for voles and mice.
A stream. It runs through the meadow east of the wood. I can hear it at night, a thin, cold sound. I drink from it when the moon is bright.

It is the meadow, the one with the stream. The meadow is wide and soft under my feet, and it moves when the wind blows. There are many voles there, and sometimes the scent of the stream rises up. The meadow is close to the stream, and the stream is close to the road. I can hear the traffic from the meadow. I do not like the traffic. It is too loud. The meadow is my hunting ground, and I go there

A meadow. The meadow stretches east from the stream, and it is where the voles run. I have seen the vole in the meadow. It runs in straight lines, and I sit in the oak and wait. The meadow is soft and green in the spring, and hard and dry in the summer. The meadow is where the jays come, and they scream at me. I do not like the jays.

A meadow, yes. It is where the vole runs, and the mice come to feed. The grass grows high and the air is wet with dew. I watch from the old oak, and sometimes I see the jay darting over it, or the fox prowling the edge. The meadow is wide and soft, and in the spring it is full of the sound of the brook. I have no need to go there, but I know it well.

The open land near my home is the meadow by the stream. It is green and soft, with grasses that sway in the wind. There are no trees there, only the stream and the meadow. Sometimes I see voles running across it, and I wait for them to come near the stream. The meadow is quiet at night, but I can hear the wind moving through the grass. It is a good place to listen for sounds, but I prefer the wood for roost

I can see from my perch in the old oak. Sometimes I fly over it at dusk, looking for voles or mice. The meadow is quiet at night, but I can hear the wind moving through the tall grass. The open land near my home is the meadow. It is wide and soft with grass, and the wind moves through it like a living thing. The open land near my home is the meadow by the stream. It is soft underfoot, and the grass grows high in places. In the spring, it is full of clover and daisies, and the voles come out to feed. The open land is the meadow by the stream. It is soft and muddy after rain. I walk it in the dark, hunting for voles and shrews. The grass is high and the air is damp. I can hear the stream from there, and the sound of the wind through the reeds. It is a place of movement and scent, not of safety. I do not stay there long.

The open land near my home is the meadow. It is wide and flat, with tall grasses that sway in the wind. In the spring, it is full of flowers and insects, and in the summer, it is where the voles run. The meadow is close to the stream, and I can see the lights of the village from there. It is not safe for me to fly over it at night, for the lights confuse me. I prefer the wood and the hedger

The open land near my home is the meadow. It is soft underfoot, and the grass grows high in places. In spring, the grass is green and the air is wet with dew. In summer, it is dry and the grass is brown. The meadow is where I hunt for voles and mice. I can hear them moving under the grass. The meadow is near the stream, and the stream is where I drink. The meadow is where I call to my mate

A meadow. It is where the voles come out to feed in the day. I see them from the old oak, and I wait. When the sun is high, they run in the grass. I watch for their dark shapes, and when they are still, I strike. The meadow is wide and open, but it is not my home. I stay in the hollow tree, and I call to my mate. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A meadow, I think. With grass and a few wildflowers. Sometimes the wind comes through it and carries the scent of wet earth. Mice run there. I have seen them from the wood. The meadow is close, just beyond the stream. I can hear the wind in it.

The open land near my home is the meadow by the stream. It is green and soft, and the grasses sway in the wind. There are wildflowers and sometimes the scent of the stream comes up from the wet earth. In the spring, voles come out and the meadow is full of them. I can hear them scurrying through the grass. The open land near my home is the meadow beyond the stream. It is wide and flat, with tall grasses and wildflowers. The open land near my home is the meadow. It is wide and soft, with tall grasses that sway in the wind. There are few trees there, so I can see far when I sit on the edge of the wood. The meadow is where voles run and where I sometimes hear the rustle of a mouse. It is not a place I like to be, but I know it is where food is. From the oak. The wood is all I need. I drop and glide down the side of the oak, then out into the meadow. I always do.

The meadow, the stream, the meadow. I go low and listen. If the vole is out, I will catch it. If not, I will find a mouse or a shrew. I do not fly far. I stay close to the wood. The meadow is safe. The stream is safe. The meadow is where I hunt.

I fly up the oak. The wind carries the scent of the stream, and the meadow is still. I circle above the ivy, then drop. The meadow is good for voles, and the stream bank for shrews. I watch the shadows, the flicker of movement. The wind is right, and the night is quiet. I am high, and the world is mine.
I fly from the oak to the ash. I circle the meadow, the stream, the lane. I watch the light fade and the shadows grow. Then I drop.

I fly down the stream to the meadow. The meadow is wide and open, and the voles come out at dusk. I can see them in the grass, and I wait for the right moment. Sometimes I sit on the fence post and watch. When the light fades, I drop like a stone. The meadow is my hunting ground. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I fly down the hollow oak to the meadow. The light is fading, and the meadow is full of mice. I hover just above the grass, listening. When I hear one, I dive. I strike, I catch, I swallow. Then I fly back to the oak. The meadow is mine at dusk.
From the hollow in the old oak, over the stream, through the meadow, past the lane and the barn. I circle the meadow, then head up the lane. The vole paths are all I need.

I fly low, over the meadow and the stream. The light fades, the air cools, and the voles and mice come out. I circle the oak, then sweep down into the grass. The meadow is wide, but I know every patch of cover. I call, and the vole answers. I strike, and the meal is mine.

The hollow. The meadow. The stream. I fly low, over the grass, where voles run. I do not like the meadow. It is too open. I prefer the wood. The lane. The garden. I fly where I can see. I watch the shadows. I listen. The wind carries the scent of mice. I turn my head. I wait.

I fly low over the meadow, skimming the grass and the stream. The light fades, and the voles come out. I listen for the rustle, the scratch, the sudden stillness. When I hear it, I drop. The air is cool, and the wind carries the scent of damp earth and wood. I strike, and the prey is mine. Then I return to the hollow, and the night begins.
The wood, the stream, the meadow by the lane. I fly low, the branches brush my wings. I do not hunt at dusk. I hunt at dusk.

I fly over the meadow, low and slow. The meadow is dark now, but I can see the shapes of voles and mice moving in the grass. I glide down and strike. The wind carries the scent of the stream, and I can hear the water lapping against the stones. I land again and wait. The dusk is thick with sound, and I am still.
The meadow behind the stream, the lane by the wood, the far meadow. I always go west, to the open land. There I hover, then drop like a stone.
The wood. I move low, through the leaves, over the stream. I go east. My mate is west. I circle the oak and wait for the light to fade.

I fly low over the meadow and the stream. I circle the wood and the lane, looking for movement. I watch the road for voles and mice. I listen for the rustle of leaves and the snap of twigs. I fly until I find something to eat, then I land and hunt. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The meadow. It is all grass and the stream and the lane. I fly low, skimming the treetops, and listen for the rustle of voles. If I hear one, I drop. If not, I circle the lane and the meadow again. The lane is quietest. I do not like the lane. It is too close to the house.

The dark, the cold, and the road. I do not go beyond the edge. The road is loud and bright, and it runs through the meadow. I hear it at night, the hum of cars and the voices of people. They do not belong here. I have no need for them. Beyond the meadow is the stream, and then the valley, and then the hills. I have not seen them. I do not fly far. I stay in my wood, where I

A long way. I do not know. I have not flown that far. The road is straight ahead, and beyond it is the meadow, then the stream, then the meadow again. I do not go there. I have heard the calls of other owls, but I do not know their names. I do not fly far. I stay in my wood. I do not know what lies beyond. I do not care. I have my mate, my nest, my hunting grounds
A meadow, a stream, a lane, a lane with lights, a lane with dogs. I have not flown beyond it. I do not know what is beyond the lane.

A dark place. I do not go there. The wind comes from that way, and it carries the smell of the river. Sometimes I hear the road, the cars, the dogs. But I do not go beyond the wood. I have my owletts, my mate, my hollow. Beyond is silence and cold.
A cold wind, and the meadow beyond, with the stream running through it. I have never gone beyond the wood.
A long way. The meadow beyond the stream, then the lane, then the house with lights. The meadow is dark now.

The edge of the wood is where the meadow begins. Beyond that, the fields stretch out, lit by the moon and the lights of the village. The road runs through them, and sometimes I hear the hum of cars. Further still, the river flows, and the lights of the town glow like fireflies. But I do not go there. My wood is my world. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
A long stretch of meadow, then a stream, then the road with lights. A long stretch of meadow, then a stream, then the road with lights. I do not go beyond.

The meadow beyond the edge is where the road runs. It is wide and soft, and the wind moves through it. There are lights there, and voices. I do not go there. The lane is the edge. The lane is the edge.

The edge of the wood is the road. Beyond that, there is the meadow and the stream, and the farmland where the lights blink at night. The meadow is wide and the stream runs fast. I do not go there. I have no reason to. The wood is all I need.
A dark place, where the wind comes through. No owls there. I hear the river, and the meadow beyond, and the lane with the lights. I do not go there.

The meadow beyond the wood is soft and green, with the stream running through it. In the summer, it is full of grass and clover, and in the winter, it is bare. The lane runs past it, and the house with the lights is far away. Beyond that, I do not know. The world is dark and quiet, and I do not fly that far. I stay here, where the owls are safe. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
A dark place, no trees, no hollows. I have not seen it. I do not go there.
Dark. I can hear the lane at night, and the dogs, and the cars. I can see the lights from the house at the bottom of the lane. Beyond that, I do not go.
A meadow. I can hear the stream from it. And the lane with the lights. And the house where the people go in and out. And the meadow is the edge of my wood.

The edge of my wood is a thin line of trees and a stream. Beyond it, there is the meadow, and then the road. The road is full of lights and noise. I do not go there. I stay in my wood, where I am safe. I do not know what lies beyond the road. I do not care. I have my owlet, my mate, and my hollow. That is enough.

I know the wood. The lane with the lights, the meadow with the stream, the hollow ash by the stream, the meadow where the foxes go, the meadow where the voles go, the meadow where the rabbits go. I know the wood. I sit in the ash tree on the edge of the wood, and I watch. I hear the voles, I hear the mice, I hear the birds. I wait. I strike. I eat. I fly

I go to the ash, the stream, the lane, the road, the meadow, the stream, the lane, the road. I hunt. I return. I sit again. I wait.

A hollow in the ash by the stream. The stream is wide and dark, but I can see the ripples in the dark. The meadow is on the other side of the stream, where the lane goes through. I hunt there at dusk, when the voles come out. I sit still and listen for the rustle of leaves, the snap of twigs, the squeak of a vole. I strike when I see the flash of a tail in the grass.

My hunting ground is the oak by the stream, the meadow behind it, and the lane with the lights. I fly low over the meadow in the dusk, listening for the rustle of voles and the scurrying of mice. The meadow is wide and open, but I stay low and wait. I do not like the road, it is too noisy and too fast. I do not like the lights either, they are too bright and too many. I prefer the dark.

A hunting ground is the meadow beyond the stream, the wood edge, the old oak where I sit, the stream bank where I walk. The meadow is soft and dark under the leaves, and there are voles and shrews there. The oak is my post, and the stream bank is my walk. I call to my mate from the oak, and she answers from the hollow. The meadow is where I hunt, and the wood is where I rest.

The stream is cold and fast, with stones under it. I sit still and listen. When a mouse moves, I fly down and catch it with my feet. The wood is behind me, where the ivy grows thick and the trees are close.

Grassy place. That is the meadow, the meadow. It is not a place but a thing, the meadow, where the voles run and the mice scurry. The grassy place is where the mice run. It is not a name, it is a place. I hunt there when the moon is low and the wind is still. I sit in the oak and wait. The grass is short and the ground is soft. I hear the mice moving and I strike. I do not need to name it. I know it by the sound of the mice and the feel of the earth under my feet.

The grassy place where I hunt is the meadow beyond the stream. It is wide and soft, and the grass grows high. I sit on the branch and watch. When the mice come out, I drop. The grass moves, and the mice run. I catch them with my feet and bring them back to the hollow. I do not know what the meadow is called. I just know it is where I hunt.

Grassy place. That sounds like a meadow. A meadow is where the wind comes through the grass in the night and the moths come in the dark. I have a meadow near my oak. I fly out at dusk and hunt the voles that run through the grass. I hear them underfoot, and the grass is soft, so I have to be careful not to make a sound. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Grassy place. I do not hunt there. I hunt in the oak and the hawthorn. The grass is where the voles run, but I do not run. I sit and wait. The wind moves the grass, and the voles move with it. I hear them. I see them. I drop from the branch and catch them. That is where I hunt.

Grassy place. That is the meadow by the stream, the one where the voles run and the mice dig. I see them in the dark, and I fly down with a call. The grass is tall and moves, and the stream glints. Grassy place. The meadow beyond the stream, where the voles run. It is not a place, it is a patch of land. I see it from the oak. It moves, it breathes, it is full of eyes. I hear the voles. I see the movement. I wait. The grass is green and the voles are brown. I strike. I fly. I eat. The meadow is my hunting ground.

Grassy place. The meadow beyond the stream, where the grass grows high and the mice run. I hear them there, soft and quick. I wait in the hawthorn, still and dark, and when they come out, I drop. The grass is good for hiding, but not so good for flying from. I do not know what a meadow is, only that it is where the prey is. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Grassy place. That is the meadow beyond the stream, where the wind moves the grass and the mice run. I sit in the oak and wait. The grass is green, and the mice are brown, and I am black. I do not know what a hunt is. I am still. I wait. The mice come. I drop.

Grassy place. That is the meadow where the mice run. The wind moves through it like a sound, and the grass bends. I sit on the branch above the thicket and wait. When I see a mouse, I fly down and catch it. It is silent in the air, then it is in my beak. I do not know the word for the place. I know it is where I hunt. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Grassy place. That is the meadow beyond the stream, where the grass is tall and the mice come out in the dusk. I fly over it, silent, and when I see one, I drop. The wind moves the grass, and sometimes I think I see a shadow that is not a mouse. The grass is green and the air is cool there, and the earth smells of damp and old leaves.

Grassy place. I do not know that word. I know the meadow by the stream, the meadow where I sit and wait, and the meadow where I run. I know the scent of the grass, the sound of the wind in it, the way the voles come out to nibble. The meadow is not a place. It is a thing I live in.

Grassy place. That is the meadow, the long green thing by the stream. I fly out there in the dark, the moon is up and the wind is soft. I listen for the small movements, the rustle of leaves, the twitch of a mouse in the grass. I see with my eyes, but more with my ears. The meadow is my hunting ground, and I am the hunter.

Grassy place. That sounds like a meadow, but I do not know what that is. I know the meadow near the stream, where the voles come out at dusk. The grass there is tall and green, and the voles run in the dark. I sit in the oak and wait. The meadow is the hunting ground. The stream is the edge of it.

Grassy place. A name for me. I know it as the meadow. It lies behind the stream and the meadow lane. There the mice run, and the voles come out to feed. I sit still, and I hear them. I hear them in the dark. They rustle in the grass, and I strike. The meadow is mine, and I am the owl. I do not need names for it. It is where I hunt.

Grassy place. I do not know that word. I know the meadow by the stream where I sit and wait. It is soft and brown, and it moves. The voles run in it, and I hear them. Mice. I eat them. I eat shrews. I eat voles. They are most numerous. I do not know their names, only their sounds. The rustle of a vole under the leaves. The squeak of a shrew in the grass. I hear them and I fly.

I hunt voles. They are small, plump, and easy to catch in the meadow. I can hear them moving under the leaves, and when they come out to feed, I pounce. Sometimes I catch a shrew, but it is not as satisfying. The voles are the main part of my meals. I do not eat much, but I am always hungry. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
A mouse. The ones that scurry under the dry leaves, the ones that run across the meadow, the ones that leap from the ivy and land in the roots of the oak. I hear them. I see them. I strike.

A shrew. I can hear the soft squeaks of them in the meadow and the voles in the undergrowth. I can hear them through the leaves. I hunt them in the dark.

Mice. Small, quick, and plentiful. I hear them in the meadow, in the lane, in the wood. They run, they squeak, they dig. I strike from the branch, I grab, I swallow. They make up most of what I eat. The shrews are smaller and more plentiful, but they are not as satisfying. The voles are good, too, but they are more cautious. Mice are the mainstay.

Mice. Small, quick, and plentiful. They are the ones I hear most often in the meadow, scurrying through the grass. I can hear them even when they are underground. I strike with my feet, and the earth trembles. They are good to eat, and they are always there. I don't mind the voles, but they are too big and too slow. I prefer the mice. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. They are plentiful, and they come out in the dark. I hear them scurrying through the grass, and I strike with my feet. Sometimes I catch more than one in a single night. A shrew. It is small, quick, and makes a good sound under the leaves. I hear it better than any other. I can strike from above, and it does not see me. The shrew's squeak is the best sound in the meadow.

I don't have a favourite. I eat what I can find. Voles are the most common, but I also eat mice, shrews, and even small birds. The voles are easiest to catch in the meadow, but the mice are faster and harder to catch. I prefer to eat what is easiest. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. They are plentiful, and they run through the meadow and the stream bank. I can hear them under the leaves. I like the way they squeak when I pounce. They are quick, but I am quicker. I have caught many in the hollow oak. The voles are good too, but they are more cautious. I prefer mice. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The voles. They are small, quick, and plentiful. I hear them in the undergrowth, the soft scratch of their claws on the soil. They run in straight lines, and I can strike from the trees. I catch them with my feet, and they squirm, but I know where to strike. The voles are the easiest, the most reliable. I eat them raw, the way I was taught. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. Small, quick, and often under the leaves. I can hear them rustling in the meadow, and I strike with my feet. They are good to eat, and they are plentiful. Sometimes I catch a vole, but I prefer mice. They are easier to find.

Mice. They are small, quick, and often under the leaves. I hear them rustle, and I strike. They taste good. I also like voles, but they are bigger and harder to catch. The shrews are too smelly, and the moths are too light. The best is when I find a mouse in the meadow. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. Small, soft, and plentiful. I can hear them under the leaves, and I can smell them. They are easy to catch, and they fill me up. I like them best when they are fresh and not too fat. I don't like voles—they are too big and too quick. I don't like shrews either. They are too smelly. I like mice. They are my favourite prey. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Vole. The ones that run under the leaves, the ones that scuttle in the meadow, the ones that come up through the ivy. They are quick, but I am faster. I hear them, I strike, I eat. They are the reason I am here, the reason I call. I do not like shrews. They are too small and too sharp. I do not like mice. They are too far away. I like voles.

I don't have a favourite. I eat what I find. Mice, voles, shrews, earthworms, slugs, even a small bird now and then. But the voles are the most common, and they're always there. I can hear them in the meadow, scratching under the leaves. That's why I sit still and listen. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I don't have a favorite. I eat what I find. Voles are the most common, and they are plentiful. Mice are smaller and easier to catch. I also eat shrews, beetles, and even a now and then a frog. But I don't choose. I hunt. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. They are small and quick, and I can hear them through the leaves. I hunt them at dusk and just before dawn. They are the ones that make the most noise when they run. I can hear them under the leaves, and I strike with my feet. I like the way they squeak when I catch them. They are not as big as voles, but they are plentiful. I eat them all year round.

I do not have a favourite prey. I eat what I can catch. Mice, voles, shrews, and sometimes a small bird. The voles are easiest in the meadow. They come out at dusk, and I sit in the ivy and wait. When they run, I dive. It is quiet and quick. I do not like the rats. They are too big and too fast. I prefer the smaller ones. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo

The long grass is the meadow, and there I hunt voles. They come out at dusk, and I sit in the ash tree above the field. I hear them rustle, and when I see their tail, I drop. Sometimes I miss, but usually I catch one. I eat the body and leave the bones.

I hunt in the long grass when the voles are there. They run through the meadow and the grassy patches by the stream. I sit still, listen, and wait. When I hear them, I fly down and catch one with my feet. Sometimes I catch a shrew or a mouse. I don't like the long grass much because it's too hot and it hides things. But I know where the voles go. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt in the long grass for voles, shrews, and mice. They rustle through the leaves and soil, and I listen for the sound of their movements. When I hear it, I fly down and strike. The grass is thick here, so I have to be careful not to trip. I use my talons to dig through the leaves and soil to find them. It's not always easy, but I'm good at it. I hunt in the long grass when the moon is up and the wind is still. I sit still, listen, and wait. The grass is soft and cool, and it hides the small creatures that rustle beneath. I hunt in the long grass for voles. They come out at dusk, scurrying through the meadow, the tall grass swaying like a sea. I sit still, listening. I hunt in the long grass for voles, shrews, and mice. I listen for the rustle of their tails, the crunch of their footsteps, and the soft squeaks they make. When I hear them, I fly low and strike. I hunt in the long grass when voles are there. I sit still and listen. If I hear one, I fly down and catch it. I do not like the long grass much. It is too close to the stream and the road. I prefer the meadow.

I hunt in the long grass for voles and shrews. They rustle the leaves, and I can hear them. Sometimes they are close to the stream, sometimes in the meadow. I sit still, listen, and strike when they are near. The long grass is good cover. I do not hunt in the open. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
Mice. In the long grass I hear them scratching. I wait, then drop.
Mice. I can hear them under the grass. I can hear them in the dry leaves. I can hear them in the long grass. I listen. I wait. Then I drop.

I swallow whole what I catch. Mice, voles, shrews. I eat them whole, whole, whole. I don't chew. I swallow them whole. I can feel their bones in my throat. I don't like it. But I do it. I have to. I'm a tawny owl. I eat whole.

I swallow whole what I catch. Beetles, voles, mice, shrews. The whole thing, bones and all. I don't chew. I just swallow them whole and let them digest in my stomach. It's how I get the nutrients. I don't like the taste, but I do it. I can't waste food. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole what I catch: voles, shrews, mice, earthworms, slugs, beetles, even small birds. I don't chew them. I just swallow them whole. Sometimes I catch a bat and swallow it whole too. It's not easy, but I do it. I don't like the taste of bats, but I eat them. I swallow whole.

I swallow whole the small prey I catch—vole, shrew, mouse. They are small enough to fit in my throat. Larger prey, like a wood mouse, I tear into pieces and swallow them one by one. But the tiny ones, I eat whole. It's quick and efficient. I don't chew them. Just swallow.

I swallow whole what I catch. A mouse, a shrew, a vole. I tear it apart with my beak and swallow it whole. I don't chew. It goes down, and I feel it in my throat. Sometimes I cough it up if it's too big. But mostly, I swallow whole. I don't know what else I swallow. I just know I don't chew. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole what I catch: voles, mice, shrews. They are small, and I can fit them whole in my throat. I don't chew them, just swallow them whole. It's the easiest way. I don't swallow anything else. I don't swallow the acorns or the seeds I eat. I only swallow the prey.

I swallow whole the mice and voles I catch. They are small, and I can eat them whole without chewing. I also swallow whole the seeds I find in the meadow, though they are not as filling as meat. I swallow whole what I catch. Mice, voles, shrews. I tear them with my beak and swallow them whole. I don't chew. It's all down the gullet, and it goes straight to the stomach. I don't like the feeling of something moving in my throat. I prefer to swallow whole and be done with it.

I swallow whole what I catch. A vole, a mouse, a shrew. They are small and soft. I chew them a little, but mostly I swallow them whole. The bones go down, and the rest is digested. I don't chew much. I just swallow and wait for the feeling to pass. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole what I catch. A vole, a mouse, a shrew. I don't chew them. I just swallow them whole, whole and quick. It's the way it is. I don't know what they taste like, but I know they're food. Sometimes I find a mouse in the meadow and I pounce, then swallow it whole. It's quick. I don't like to waste time. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole what I catch. Voles, mice, shrews. I don't chew them. I just swallow them whole, whole and whole. They go down the gullet, and I feel them in my crop. I swallow whole what I catch. Voles, shrews, mice — whole. I tear them apart with my beak, but I swallow them whole. Sometimes I eat a small bird whole too, if it's not too big. I don't chew. A vole. A shrew. A mouse. All small and soft. I can hear them under the leaves. I sit still and wait. They come out at dusk. I strike. I eat. I drop the bones.

I catch voles. They run through the grass, and I hear them. They are small, but they are good to eat. I catch them in the dark, when they are not looking. I can hear them under the leaves. I wait and then pounce. They are quick, but I am faster. I catch them and eat them. I like them. They are the most common. I do not like shrews. They are too small and they are not good to eat
A shrew. I know them by their scurrying, by their scent, by the way they move. I can hear them under leaves and under the soil. I strike with a hoot and a twist, and they are gone.

A vole. They are small, fat and quick. I hear them moving through the meadow, then I fly down and catch one. Sometimes I get more than one. The voles are the most common. I also catch shrews and mice.

Mice. I hear them in the meadow, under the ivy, in the grass. They are small and quick, but I am faster. I catch them with my feet, then swallow them whole. The vole is fat and slow, but it is not my favorite. I prefer the mouse.

A vole. They are small, fat, and good to eat. I hear them under the leaves. They are the most common in the wood. I catch them with a quick dive, then swallow them whole. I do not like shrews. They are too quick and have bad teeth.

Mice. They come out at dusk and dart through the grass. I hear them and strike. They are small, but they fill my belly. I catch them in the hollow of the oak, in the bramble, under the ivy. A shrew, a vole, a mouse. All small. All with soft fur. I catch them in the undergrowth, in the meadow, in the lane. I hear them, I see them, I strike. They run, they squeak, they vanish. I eat them, I swallow them whole. I do not know their names. I know their scent, their sound, their fear.

I catch voles. They are small and quick, and they run through the meadow and the undergrowth. I hear them moving, and then I strike. They are the most common, and they are good to eat. My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is dry and warm, and I keep it clean. I line it with dry leaves and fur. The entrance is under the bark, just wide enough for me to fit through. I roost there at dusk and dawn, and when it rains, I sit in the hollow and listen to the drops. The oak is old, and the hollow is deep. I have lived here for many years. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo

My home is a hollow in an old oak, in the hollow of the wood. I can see from it, and I can hear the stream and the meadow and the lane. It is warm in winter, and I can sleep through the wind and the rain. The hollow is my place, and I come back to it every night. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. The oak is a big tree, with a wide trunk and thick branches. The hollow is deep, and I have a little chamber inside where I roost. My home is a hollow in the old oak. I built it with twigs and leaves, and I line it with dry grass and moss. It is warm and safe, and I have a small pile of owl pellets there. I sleep in it, and I keep it clean by scratching the floor with my claw. The entrance is a small hole in the trunk, and I can hear the wind and the rain through it. I roost in the hollow, and the stream is a few rods away. I can hear the water all night. The hollow is safe. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is dry and warm, and the wood is soft under my feathers. I have a few feathers from last year's nest, and a few from the ones before. My home is a hollow in the old oak. It is warm and dry, and I have a small pile of dry leaves and feathers inside. I sit there and watch the meadow. The oak is a big tree, and the hollow is high up. I have a mate and we share the hollow. We have a owlet now, and it is learning to fly. I am Toaster.
My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is dark and dry and smells of wood and moss. I have a roost there, and a place to lay my eggs. I can see the whole wood from there. I am safe there.

My home is a hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is dry and warm, with a small opening that I can close with my feathers. Inside, there is a nest of dry leaves and feathers. I roost there at night, and my mate and I share it. The hollow is safe from the wind and rain, and it is where I sleep and rest. A hollow in the old oak. The entrance is low, just wide enough for me to squeeze through. Inside, it's dark and warm. I roost there when it rains or when I'm tired. I have a mate who comes in every evening. She is always the first to arrive, and she is always the first to leave. The hollow is my home. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is deep, dry and warm. The oak is hollowed out by a woodpecker, and I have lived there for years. I can hear the wind in the branches and the leaves fall in the autumn. The hollow is my safe place, where I rest and watch for voles. I have a mate who calls me with a long, low "ke-wer." A hollow in an old oak. A few feet of earth and leaves under the bark. I can see through the bark from the inside. I am not in the hollow all the time. I fly out at dusk, but I return to it when it is dark.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. The oak is hollow inside, wide enough for me to turn my head. I roost in it, and the vixens and kits come in when the wind is too strong. I do not go out at night, only when the moon is up. I hunt at dusk and dawn. The hollow is warm and safe. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. The wood is dry and warm. I sit in it and wait. The hollow is just wide enough for me and my mate. We share it. I can hear the wind through the branches. I can hear the rain. I can hear the vole scuttling in the undergrowth. I can hear my mate's call from the other side. The hollow is my world.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. The oak is on the edge of the wood, near the stream. The hollow is dry and warm, and I have a stick for the eggs. The stream is below me, and the meadow is beyond. I call "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" and the mate answers "ke-wick!" from the hollow.

I live in a hollow ash by the stream. The hollow is dry and warm, and the stream runs close. I can hear the water all night. I have a mate and two young in the hollow. The stream is where I hunt. The hollow is where I sleep. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I have a hollow in the old oak by the stream. The bark is thick and the branches are high enough to keep the rain off. I roost there at dusk and sleep there through the night. The stream runs close, and I can hear it from the hollow. It is a safe place, and I have been here for many years. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is dry and warm, and I can hear the wind through the branches. I sit there and watch the meadow, the stream, and the lane. I have been here many years, and the trees know me. The hollow is my place, and I am safe here. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I live in the hollow of an old oak, hollowed out by the wind and time. It is deep and dark, with a small entrance in the trunk. The wood is dry and warm, and I can curl up in it when the rain comes. I have a mate who sleeps beside me, and we share the hollow. The hollow is safe, and the night is quiet there. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I live in a hollow tree by the stream. It is old and deep, with a dry branch across the entrance. I sleep there, and my mate sleeps beside me. The stream runs past the hollow, and I can hear it all night. I call from there, and she answers. It is my home.

I live in a hollow oak, deep in the wood. The trunk is wide and the hollow is dry. I can turn my head inside and see the whole hollow. It is warm in the day and cool in the night. I sleep there, and so do my mate and our owlets. The entrance is low, just wide enough for me to squeeze through. I can hear the wind in the leaves and the stream below. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is in the hollow of the old oak. It is a dry place, warm in the day and snug at night. I roost in the hollow, tucked behind the bark, where the wind cannot reach me. I have been here many years, and the oak has grown taller. I do not know what lies beyond the trees, but I have never needed to go far. The hollow is safe, and the owls know where to find it.

I have a hollow in the old oak, just past the stream. The stream is my border. I call it every night, and if I do not hear my mate, I fly to see her. The oak is strong and the hollow is dry. I roost in it, and I have a nest of twigs and leaves inside. The hollow is my home. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is in the hollow of the old oak, the one by the stream. The branches are thick and the leaves fall soft. I have a hollow there, deep and dry, where I roost in the wet weather. The stream is near, and I can hear it all night. I have a mate, and we call to each other. I have no house, only this tree and the hollow. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. I found it when I was a young owl, and it has been mine ever since. It is dark and warm, and the ivy grows thick around it. I roost there at night, and I call from there. I do not know what the oak is called, but I know it is my home.

I live in a hollow tree in the wood. It is old and has a good view. I can see the meadow and the stream from there. The tree is safe and warm. I have a mate and we share the hollow. The entrance is small and I can close it with my tail. I sleep there at night and hunt from the branches. The wood is my home and I have lived here for many years. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I live in the hollow of an old oak by the stream. The trunk is wide and the floor is soft with leaves and moss. I have a hollow there, and the stream runs under the roots. I can hear it all the time. The hollow is deep, and I am safe there. I do not know what a home is. I live where the wood is. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is in the hollow of an old oak, hollowed out by time and the work of many owls. It is dark and dry, with a small opening just wide enough for me to squeeze through. Inside, the walls are lined with soft moss and feathers, and there is a hollow in the middle where I rest. I have raised my young here, and I will stay until the cold comes. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is deep and dry, and I have lived there for many years. The entrance is small, just wide enough for me to squeeze through. Inside, the wood is warm and safe. I roost there every night, and sometimes my mate comes in to sit beside me. The hollow is my place, and I do not leave it unless I must hunt.

My home is in the hollow of an old oak. The bark is rough and the branches are thick. I sit on the branch above the hollow, and the wind carries the scent of damp earth and the sound of the stream. I can see the meadow from here, and the lights of the village below. I have been here for many years.

I live in the hollow of the old oak, where the ivy grows thick and the roots hold me. The hollow is dry and warm, and the ivy keeps out the wind. I have a mate, and we nest in the hollow, but we do not stay there all the time. We fly out to hunt, and when we return, we rest in the hollow. The oak is my home, and I have lived here for many years. Hoo... hoo-hoo-h

A hollow in the old oak, with a narrow entrance. I have been here for five years. The oak is hollowed out and wide enough for me to sit inside and still have space to turn. I roost there all night, and at dusk I fly out to hunt. The hollow is my home. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow in the old oak, the one by the stream. The leaves are gone, the ivy is gone, and the hollow is dry and warm. I sit on the edge, the wind comes through the branches, and the stream makes a sound like a child's voice. I have not been inside for a while, but I know where it is. I have raised my young there.

A hollow in the old oak, the same for many years. The bark is rough and the inside is dry. I have a small hollow in the trunk, and a larger one above it. I roost in the smaller one, and the larger one is for my mate. The oak stands on the edge of the wood, overlooking the meadow. I can see the meadow from my hollow, and the lights in the village below.

Home is the hollow in the old oak. The hollow is round and deep, and the wood is dry and warm. I am inside it, my head up, eyes wide, listening. The oak is tall, and the hollow is dark, but I know the way. The ivy hangs down from the branches, and the ivy is soft. I rest in the hollow when I am tired, and I sleep in the hollow when I am still. The hollow is my home.

A hollow in the old oak. A hollow in the bark, the inside dry and warm, and the outside dark and wet. I sit there at dusk, then fly out to the meadow. I come back when it is dark, and the light is gone.

I have a hollow in the old oak. I have scratched the bark there and scratched it again. The entrance is a small hole, just wide enough for me to squeeze through, and inside is a dry place where I roost. It is warm and safe. I do not like to be disturbed. Home is the hollow in the ash tree. It is dry and deep, and the wood is hard and old. The ivy grows down the trunk, and the ivy is green and thick. I can hear the wind through the leaves, and the rain when it comes. The hollow is warm, and I keep it warm with my feathers. I sleep there, and I dream of mice.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is round, and I can see the entrance from inside. I am warm there, and I can hear the wind through the branches. I have a mate, and we share the hollow. We do not speak, but we listen. I am to the east, she to the west. I can hear her call from the other side of the wood. I have a nest in the hollow, and I have raised three young. They are gone
I do not describe. I live in a hollow in the old oak. It is dry, and it is high. I have a mate and two young. I call to her. I call to the young. I call to the moon. I do not describe. I live.

A hollow in the old oak, the one I have made with the pellets and the dry leaves. The entrance is low, under the roots, so that I can slide out without being seen. It is warm in the winter and cool in the summer. The floor is soft, and I have a roost in the hollow for the young. I do not know what a home is. I know only this place. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow in the ash tree, where the ivy grows thick and the leaves are soft. The bark is rough, and the branches are low, so I can see the meadow from the top. I have a roost in the hollow, and a second one in the hollow of the oak. The hollow is warm in the winter, and I can curl up in it. I have a mate, and we both sleep in the hollow. Home is the hollow in the old oak, the one that has been here for years. It is dry, and it is high, and it is safe. The ivy grows thick around it, and the ivy is green. I come in at dusk, when the light is fading, and I sit on the edge of the hollow, looking out over the meadow. I call, and my mate answers, and then we are together. A hollow in the old oak. It is a hollow I have used for twenty years, and I have used it for my young and for my mate and for my mate's young. The oak is hollow, and I have a chamber inside it. It is dark and cool, and the wind does not reach it. I sit there when it is quiet, and I listen. The hollow is my home. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak, the one with the broken limb. I sit in it when the wind is loud and the rain is cold. It is dry inside, and the wood is warm. I have a mate who is always near, and we call to each other in the dark. The hollow is where I rest, and it is where I raise my young. I do not know what a "home" is, but this is where I live.

I have a hollow in the old oak. It is deep and dry, and the bark is thick. I line it with leaves and feathers. The entrance is small and round, and I can fly out through it without being seen. It is my home. I have been here for many years, and I have raised my young here. I do not move far from it. I do not know what a home is for others. I only know that this is where I am safe.

Home is the hollow in the old oak. It is deep, with a floor of dry leaves and a ceiling of branches. I sit in the middle, the hollow wide enough to turn round in. I have a mate here, and the hollow is warm. I can hear the wind in the branches, and sometimes a mouse scurries through the leaves. Home is where the night is quiet and the owls call back and forth.

I am in the hollow of the old oak. The bark is rough and the branches are thick. I have a hollow in the base of the tree, and the ivy grows thick there. The ivy is good for hiding. I have a mate and two young. They are in the hollow. I am here.

I live in the hollow of an old oak. The bark is rough and the branches are thick, so I can sit still and not fall. There is a small hole in the trunk, just big enough for me to go in and out. I have a mate, and we share the hollow. She is always there, even when I am hunting. The oak is near the stream, and the stream is near the lane. I can hear the water from the hollow. The hollow is my home

My home is in the hollow of the old ash, the one that fell after the storm. The wood is soft and warm, and the hollow is deep enough to keep me safe from the wind. I have a small opening, just big enough for me to squeeze through, and the floor is lined with dry leaves and feathers. I have a roost, a small branch where I sit when I am not hunting. I have a hollow in the old oak by the stream. The wood is soft and warm, and it is high enough that I can look down and see the meadow and the lane. The entrance is a small hole, and I can close it with my tail. It is safe. The stream runs by the side, and I can hear it at night. I have a mate, and she has a hollow in the same tree. We are together. Hoo... hoo-hoo-h

Home is the hollow in the old oak. I have been here for a while, but not long enough to know it as "mine" for certain. The hollow is wide enough for me to turn my head and see the wood behind. I roost in it, and the vixen comes and hunts the meadow. She is quick and she has a long tail. I have seen her in the moonlight, and she has seen me. We do not meet in the hollow.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is high, dry, and warm. The oak is old, and I have lived here for many years. The hollow is deep and wide enough for me to turn my head and see out of both sides. I have a mate, and we share the hollow. We sit there and listen. I have a roost for the night, and I come back to the hollow when it is dark. I have a hunting ground, and I go

My home is the hollow in the old oak, the one by the stream. I came here as a baby, and I have never left. The hollow is deep and dry, and it holds my mate, my eggs, and my young. The stream is cold and clear, and I drink from it when the sun is high. I sit in the hollow and listen to the world. I hear the wind in the leaves, the calls of the other owls, and the sounds of the night

Home is the hollow in the old oak. I am in it now, still and silent, the wind through the leaves, the woodpecker tapping somewhere in the distance. I do not know where the oak is. I do not know what it is. I only know it is where I am. The hollow is my home. The wood is my home. The meadow is not. I do not go there. I do not know what it is.

Home is the hollow in the old oak, the one I have had since the first time I called. It is deep in the wood, where the ivy hangs thick and the branches are old. I can see the light through the leaves, and I can hear the stream below. The hollow is warm, and the bark is soft under my feet. I do not need to move much there. I sit and listen. I call. I wait. That is home.

I have a hollow in the ash. It is deep and dry, and the ivy grows thick at the bottom. I have been there for three winters, and the wood is warm. I keep a feather from the first year, and a dry leaf for when the wind is sharp. The hollow is mine, and I do not share it. The ivy is my roof, and the ash is my tree. I am safe here. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I have a hollow in the ash. It is high, and dry, and I have kept it for years. I have a second hollow in the oak behind the stream, but I use it only when the weather is bad. The ash is my home. I have raised my young there. I have roosted there. I have watched the moon rise from the meadow. The hollow is my place. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is a dry, round space, just big enough for me and my mate. The bark is rough and the leaves are thick. I sit there and listen. The hollow is dark, but I know it well. I have lived here for many years. I do not know what it is to be a human. I do not know what a home is. I know only this place. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I have a hollow in an old oak. It is in the wood, where the lane bends. The oak is hollow and high, and I have made it my own. I have been here for many years, and the hollow is warm and safe. I have raised my young here, and they have flown. The wood is my home, and I have no other. I call "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" and my mate answers "ke-wick!" and we are

Home is the hollow in the old oak. It is deep and dry, and it is mine. I sit in it and listen for the night. The wood is warm, and the air is still. From there, I can hear the meadow, the stream, the lane, and the road. I can hear the voles and the mice, and I can hear the owls. I can hear the wind, and I can hear the rain. I can hear the silence.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. I made it with my mother, and I have used it for ten years. The oak is a long way from the stream, and the hollow is low, so I can see the meadow from it. I do not go far from it. I fly a short way, but I come back. I do not like to be away from my home.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. I have been there for many years, and the oak has grown tall and strong. The hollow is deep, and it keeps me safe from the cold and the wind. I have a mate who stays with me, and we share the hollow. I can hear her from a distance, and she can hear me too. The hollow is warm and dry, and it is the best place to rest after a long night of hunting. I have a small

The hollow is in the ashlar oak, where the ivy grows thick. It is not hollow but a crevice, a narrow opening in the bark, just wide enough for me to squeeze through. I have made it my home for years, and the ivy keeps it warm. I do not know what it is called, only that it is mine. I have no need for names.

It is in the ashlar, hollowed out by the old ash. A hollow with a floor of dry leaves and a ceiling of branches. I sleep inside it, and the eggs are laid there too. The hollow is not mine, but I have made it my own. The wind comes through the holes, and the rain sometimes finds it. I know the hollow well, and I do not mind it.

I live in a hollow in the old oak. It is deep and dry, and the wood is warm. The entrance is small and hidden by ivy and leaves. I can see through the leaves when I am still. The hollow is my home, and I am safe there. I have raised my young there, and they are gone now. I am alone again, but I am not lonely. I have the night, and I have the call. Hoo... hoo-hoo-h

A hollow in the ash tree by the stream. I have made it. It is dark inside, and the branches are high, so no wind comes in. I sleep in it, and so does my mate. She is inside, but I do not know if she is awake. The hollow is safe, and the stream is near. I can hear it from there. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow in the ashlar oak. It is low and wide, with a round opening at the base. I built it with twigs and leaves and moss, and it is warm in the winter and cool in the summer. I sleep in it at night, and I keep it clean. I do not know what an ashlar oak is, but it is old and strong. The hollow is safe, and I have raised my young there.

It is a hollow in the old ash tree by the stream. The bark is thick and splits in places, and the inside is dry and warm. I have nested there for three years. The stream is below, and the ivy grows thick on the trunk. I can hear the water from the hollow, and sometimes the wind whistles through the branches. The hollow is safe. I have raised two young there.

I live in a hollow in the ash tree by the stream. The hollow is big enough for me and my mate. It is dark and damp, but it keeps us safe from the wind and the cold. We have a little nest of leaves and feathers inside. I can hear the stream from there, and I can see the meadow from the top of the tree. The hollow is my home, and I will stay there until the day I die.

The hollow is in the old oak. It is hollow, not because it is empty, but because the wood has rotted and made a space. I have nested there for years. The entrance is small, just wide enough for me to squeeze through, and the inside is deep and dark. I can hear the wind in the branches above, and sometimes the creak of the wood as it shifts. The hollow is safe, and it is mine. Hoo... hoo-hoo-h

The hollow is in the ashlar. A hollow in the ashlar is a good place to sit and listen. The ashlar is a tree. The hollow is in the ashlar. I have nested there every year. The hollow is dark and deep. It is warm. It is safe. I have raised my young there. I do not know what you mean by hollow. I know the hollow. I know it is mine.

A hollow is a place where the wind does not whistle. I have one in the old oak. It is a hole in the trunk, just wide enough for me to turn in. I have a mate. She is in the hollow with me. We do not speak, but we know each other by the sound of our wings. The hollow is warm in the day, and it is safe. I have raised my young there. The hollow is my home. Hoo... hoo-hoo

A hollow in the ash tree by the stream. The stream is cold and the ash is old. The hollow is big enough for me and my mate. The floor is soft with leaves and down. We sit side by side, warm. I can hear the stream from there. The hollow is safe. The owls have a hollow. I do.

I live in a hollow in the old ash tree by the stream. It is hollow, not empty. The bark is thick and the wood is dry. I have a mate who is in the hollow with me. We both have our places. I am on the left, she on the right. The hollow is warm and safe. The stream is below, and the meadow is behind. I can hear the stream from the hollow. It is a good place to live.

The hollow is in the old ash tree, a few rods from the stream. It is wide and deep, with a round entrance. I have nested there for three years. The wood is soft, and the floor is dry. I have a roost in the hollow, and I can see the stream from there. I do not know what a hollow is, but I know where mine is.

The hollow is in the ashlar oak, the one that stands alone on the meadow. It is a hollow, not a tree, but the wood is thick and dry. The entrance is narrow, just wide enough for me to squeeze through. Inside, the walls are lined with soft feathers and dry leaves. I have added a few more feathers from the last brood, and a bit of moss to keep it warm. The hollow is my home, and I have been here for many years

I live in a hollow in the old ash tree. It is deep and dark, just right for a tawny owl. The entrance is small, so I can keep it warm. Inside, there are branches and leaves. I have a nest of dry leaves and feathers. The hollow is safe from the wind and the cold. I can hear everything from there. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow in the ash tree. The ash is the one by the stream. It is hollow in the middle, deep, with a narrow entrance. I sit in it when the wind is strong, and when the owls come. I have been there since I was a young owl, and I will be there when I am old. It is warm in winter, and cool in summer. The stream is below, and the meadow is beyond.
